d: a person or group affected by a decision or having an interest in it
ex: All key stakeholders were invited to comment on the new plan.

d: a situation in which neither side can make progress
ex: Talks between the two companies reached a stalemate after weeks of meetings.

d: a particular opinion or attitude that someone takes on an issue
ex: The board took a firm stance against any form of bribery.

d: the high level of respect someone has earned in their field
ex: The professor's international stature attracted students from many countries.

d: a strong feeling of shame or disapproval attached to something
ex: There is still a stigma attached to mental illness in many communities.

d: something that encourages activity or growth
ex: The government hopes its spending will provide a stimulus for small businesses.

d: a requirement stated clearly in an agreement or contract
ex: One stipulation of the lease is that no pets may be kept indoors.

d: a large supply of something kept for future use
ex: The city built a stockpile of salt to use during icy weather.

d: conflict or serious disagreement between people or groups
ex: Years of strife left the village divided and poor.

d: money given by the government to lower the cost of something
ex: The subsidy helps families pay for school books and uniforms.

d: the process of taking over a job, title or position from someone else
ex: The family business needs a clear plan for succession.

d: the state of being more powerful or important than all others
ex: The company held market supremacy for two decades before its rivals caught up.

d: an amount that is left over after everything needed has been used
ex: The country recorded a trade surplus for the third year running.

d: a person or thing that takes the place of another
ex: Online classes became a surrogate for lessons that were cancelled.

d: close observation of a person or place, usually by the authorities
ex: The police kept the warehouse under constant surveillance for a month.

d: the state of being easily affected or harmed by something
ex: Her susceptibility to colds increased during long periods of stress.

d: food and other things that people need in order to stay alive
ex: The relief teams brought basic sustenance to families cut off by the flood.

d: a formal meeting where experts present and discuss a subject
ex: Researchers from twelve countries attended the symposium on water management.

d: a group of people working together, often for illegal purposes
ex: Police broke up a syndicate that had been selling stolen car parts.

d: a positive effect when two or more things work better together
ex: The merger created synergy between the two teams and reduced costs.

d: the combination of separate ideas or parts into one whole
ex: The essay offers a useful synthesis of several recent studies.

d: to prevent something from growing, developing or being expressed
ex: Strict rules can stifle creativity among young designers.

d: to encourage something to start or grow more actively
ex: Lower interest rates may stimulate spending and investment in the economy.

d: to provide evidence that proves a claim is true
ex: The journalist could not substantiate the claims made in the article.

d: to weaken or undermine a system, rule or authority from within
ex: Bribery can subvert the fair process of awarding public contracts.

d: to replace an earlier rule, plan or method with a newer one
ex: The new regulations will supersede all previous guidance on safety.

d: to form an idea about something from limited information
ex: From the footprints, the police surmised that two people had left the house.

d: to be better or greater than something else
ex: Sales this year surpassed all our expectations by a wide margin.

d: to keep something going for a long time, or to support it
ex: A healthy diet can sustain energy levels throughout a long working day.

d: to cheat someone out of money in a dishonest way
ex: The gang swindled elderly people out of their savings with fake offers.

d: to influence someone's opinion or decision
ex: Strong evidence should sway the jury more than emotional appeals do.

d: to combine separate ideas or facts into one coherent whole
ex: The report synthesises findings from dozens of studies on sleep.

d: to make a process simpler and more efficient
ex: The new software will streamline the process of booking appointments.

d: to stop growing or developing and become dull
ex: Wages have stagnated for years, despite rising living costs.

d: to come from or be caused by something
ex: Many of the problems stem from poor communication between departments.

d: to be enough for a particular purpose
ex: A short summary will suffice for the first draft of the report.

d: to become less strong or less intense
ex: The protests subsided once the council agreed to listen to residents.

d: to bring something under control, often by force
ex: Security guards quickly subdued the intruder before he reached the vault.

d: to include something within a larger category or idea
ex: The new theory subsumes several older explanations of market behaviour.

d: not moving, flowing or developing, and often unhealthy
ex: Stagnant water in the old pond attracted mosquitoes.

d: loyal, reliable and strongly supportive of a cause
ex: She was a stalwart supporter of the library for thirty years.

d: very plain, clear or severe, without any comfort
ex: The report paints a stark picture of life in the flooded villages.

d: strict, demanding and carefully enforced
ex: The bank applies stringent checks before approving large loans.

d: happening or coming after something else
ex: The subsequent investigation found no evidence of fraud.

d: more than is needed or useful, and therefore unnecessary
ex: The editor removed several superfluous words from the paragraph.

d: involving only the outer or obvious parts, not the deeper meaning
ex: The article gave only a superficial account of a complex issue.

d: added to something in order to complete or improve it
ex: Students can read supplementary material on the course website.

d: affecting a very large number of things or people
ex: The new law brings sweeping changes to the way schools are funded.

d: requiring a lot of physical or mental effort
ex: Climbing the mountain was strenuous, but the view was worth the effort.

d: affecting a whole system or organisation rather than one part
ex: The audit found systemic weaknesses in how contracts were approved.

d: having the same meaning, or closely associated with something
ex: For many people, the brand has become synonymous with quality.

d: happening or done after something else
ex: The company later admitted the error and subsequently repaid the customers.

d: to a large extent or by a large amount
ex: House prices have risen substantially since the start of the decade.

d: in a way that is not immediately obvious or easy to notice
ex: The advertisement subtly suggests that the product will improve your health.

d: in a firm and loyal way, without changing
ex: The team steadfastly defended its position despite strong criticism.
